title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We conducted a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) to measure whether inserting an executable emulator validator and a bounded repair policy (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge/core/leaf–spine) we generated a single shared candidate per task with gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and scored that identical candidate under both conditions with a deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) enforcing structured workflow policies. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces record repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We (1) present a concise formal definition of the binary outcome mapping used in analysis, (2) synthesize nearest prior work in a compact comparison, (3) interpret the degenerate ceiling result in light of the shared-generation design choice, and (4) give artifact-grounded methodological recommendations for follow-ups that can meaningfully exercise repair behavior.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can translate operator intent into concrete network configuration commands, promising productivity gains for NetOps. However, syntactically plausible commands can violate stateful workflow constraints (for example, performing MTU changes without required shutdowns or causing make-before-break uplink regressions) and produce semantic failures visible only in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore recommends verifier/emulator or veto-layer integration to intercept such errors before enactment. Our preregistered confirmatory question was: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design (one generator output per task, evaluated under both conditions). We explicitly preregistered this trade-off: shared-generation removes generator variance and isolates validator marginal effects, but it reduces the probability of observing repair activity when the generator produces valid candidates for the chosen task bank.
sections.related_work:
Two complementary literatures frame our study. First, executable-benchmark and closed-loop emulation work (e.g., NetConfArena; Aether; NetOps executable benchmarks) show that closed-loop tests reveal stateful sequencing and availability errors missed by syntax-only checks. Second, tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (generate→validate→repair, veto layers, digital twins) are repeatedly proposed to improve operational safety. Prior empirical studies commonly conflate generator variability and verification efficacy because they sample independent generator outputs per condition. Our study complements these by holding the generator fixed via a shared-candidate design and reporting artifact-grounded execution traces and deterministic reconciliation.

Nearest-work comparison (compact):
- Protogeros et al. (Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair, arXiv 2604.22513): bench-focused; evaluates repair behaviors but typically uses independent generation per test; differs from our shared-candidate paired isolation.
- NetConfArena (arXiv 2608.23179): provides executable closed-loop tasks and highlights stateful failure classes; shares our emphasis on emulation but differs in experimental design choices and focus on multi-model comparisons.
- Aether (arXiv 2604.18233): agentic AI + digital twin validation; aligns on tool-augmented architectures but is more architectural/prototypical than our preregistered paired confirmatory run.
- MeshAgent (SIGCOMM/related; DOI 10.1145/3771567): addresses reliable management with LLMs and emphasizes operationalization; contrasts with our controlled, artifact-rich confirmatory framing.
This paper's distinguishing methodological contribution is the preregistered, artifact-anchored, shared-generation paired design that cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects and archives deterministic reconciliation artifacts supporting transparent interpretation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 prior to execution. Key preregistered elements: paired-binary confirmatory design (N=120 tasks; deterministic partition into edge/core/leaf–spine: 40 tasks each), primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, exact two-sided McNemar test, bootstrap-percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729), repair budget ≤1 repair per guarded episode, deterministic emulator resets and contamination controls, and explicit exclusion rules for technical/instrumentation failures. Planned_episode_count = 240 (two episodes per pair); completed_episode_count = 240; failed_episode_count = 0.

Task generation and candidate production. Tasks were deterministic synthetic intent→configuration items produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest includes initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, and an explicit required_sequence encoding canonical ordered operations (e.g., shut→configure→restore) used by the validator as structured constraints. For each pair we performed one shared initial generation using the declared model gpt-5-mini (execution recorded model_calls_used = 120; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 120) and then evaluated that identical candidate under baseline and guarded scorers.

Validator, scoring rule, and binary outcome definition. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable emulator-based validator that enforces structured workflow policies present in the task payload (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, make-before-break, final_group_constraints). The scorer applied the rule named "full_intent_constraint_validation" and emitted a structured validator_trace with fields: validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and validation_after.valid.

Formal binary outcome mapping used in the confirmatory test (explicit and artifact-grounded):
- PASS (binary label = 1) if and only if validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.violation_count == 0 AND scoring field score == 1 under scorer_id deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0).
- FAIL (binary label = 0) otherwise. Repair was triggered only when validator_trace.violation_count > 0; repaired_final_configuration and repair_applied were recorded when present.

Concrete example from archived artifacts (pair-000001): the shared candidate (normalized_response) is:
"interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up"
The corresponding scorer fields in execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and ...-guarded.json: score = 1; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; violation_count = 0; repair_applied = false. This concrete mapping defines the pass/fail labels used by the McNemar analysis.
sections.results:
Execution and primary outcome. The harness completed without technical exclusions: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120. Condition-level summaries: baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (analysis/condition_summary.csv). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces indicate repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes; no repair_provider_trace artifacts were generated.

Per-topology counts (from the task manifest and scoring artifacts):
- Edge (40 pairs): baseline 40/40 success; guarded 40/40 success.
- Core (40 pairs): baseline 40/40 success; guarded 40/40 success.
- Leaf–spine (40 pairs): baseline 40/40 success; guarded 40/40 success.

Contamination and missingness. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero technical exclusions. Deterministic_reconciliation confirms provider-call accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cache_miss_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false) and pair accounting consistency.

Interpretation of the degenerate interval. The shared-generation paired design isolates validator marginal effects by construction; when the single shared candidate satisfies the validator for every task, the guarded subsystem has no opportunity to apply repairs. The observed zero discordant pairs (n_10 = n_01 = 0) causes the exact McNemar p = 1.0 and a degenerate bootstrap CI (all resamples reproduce the same concordant table). This degenerate statistical outcome is an exact, artifact-traceable consequence of the observed data and the preregistered resampling scheme (bootstrap_seed = 1729; bootstrap_resamples = 10000).
sections.discussion:
Ceiling result implications. The ceiling (100% success in both conditions) documents a boundary case: the shared-generation design successfully isolates validator/repair marginal effects but can render the primary confirmatory test uninformative when the generator is highly calibrated for the task bank. This outcome does not imply that validators are unnecessary in general; rather, it highlights the interaction between experimental design and generator error incidence.

Design recommendations grounded in archived manifest difficulty metadata: (1) Use independent per-condition generation in confirmatory arms to expose generator variance and allow guards to intercept invalid outputs; (2) stratify or oversample "very_hard" tasks or tasks with dependency_rule_count ≥ 2 (fields present in each task_manifest entry) to raise base-line failure incidence; (3) prespecify controlled prompt perturbations for a subset of paired blocks to increase sampled generator errors while keeping other blocks paired for internal control; (4) consider exploratory arms with extended repair budgets (multiple repair iterations) to study repair convergence and cost. These concrete adjustments are directly actionable using the archived task_manifest difficulty fields and do not require new unarchived evidence.

Operational and audit implications. Even when idle, deterministic validators that emit structured traces (validation_before/after, violation codes, parsed_command_count) support operator auditability and post-hoc diagnostics. The archived execution artifacts demonstrate provider-call audits and deterministic reconciliation that can serve as the basis for operator-facing explanations and independent third-party audits in deployments where generators sometimes err.

Threats to validity (concise). Internal validity: strong (deterministic resets, complete accounting, zero exclusions). Construct validity: constrained by synthetic task payloads and validator policy encoding; not all vendor-specific behaviors or partial-observability scenarios are modeled. External validity: limited to the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline failure ≈0.40; target reduction 0.15) were violated by observed baseline = 0.00, rendering the prespecified confirmatory test infeasible for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment that compared an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow while holding the generator fixed. All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding identical 100% success rates and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The main scientific contribution is methodological: the preregistered shared-generation paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects and—together with the archived validator traces, task manifests, and deterministic reconciliation artifacts—supports reproducible interpretation of degenerate outcomes. Follow-up confirmatory designs should (and can) leverage the archived difficulty metadata to increase generator-induced error incidence (independent generation, targeted hard-task strata, controlled prompt perturbations) so that future runs can meaningfully measure repair utility in conditions where generators sometimes fail. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived and checksummed in the execution and analysis manifests referenced in the Disclosure Statement and in the manuscript evidence bundle.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
